Being a unique take on the cooking party game genre, Cook, Serve, Delicious 2 makes a huge improvement from the first installment:
- Two-player co-op is actually co-op rather than separating the control into two parts.
- Gorgeous food artwork that made you wish you can eat them in real life.
- Way fewer down time.
- Default difficulty is challenging enough without needing to crank up the difficulty.

However, this is the type of game that you would find it decent in the first few hours, but due to the nature of its gameplay design, it exposes its flaws very soon.

The first problem that stands out is the in-game ingredient key-mapping. The key per ingredient default setting is very arbitrary and has no consistency whatsoever. Sometimes it uses the first letter of the food and sometimes it tries to remain consistency with other dishes having the same ingredient, so when you combine different food that has ingredient keys mapped in a different logic, it becomes very annoying. Luckily, there is key-mapping setting for every individual food, which brings the second problem.

The second problem is that the key-mapping settings is so inconvenient and frustrating to use, to a point that it feels that the developers don't want the players to re-map their terrible default key mappings. In order to set the ingredient key-mapping to one's preference, you need to go to the food catalog, which has every single recipe listed, find the food for which the ingredient keys you want to re-map, enter practice mode to make the food yourself, and then you can re-map the keys during the practice. There is no "food search" function in the food catalog, which means you have to go through every single food if you want to remap that one dish which has key-mappings you want to change! The existing filter system is next to useless because you are never sure what arbitrary category each food is put into. Also, keys for the chores cannot be remapped for no good reason whatsoever.

I absolutely despise this game purely for the key-mapping settings in the game. It is designed to be as inconvenient as possible. I am not recommending this game purely out of this reason, but I am not done yet.

The third problem is that the requirement for gold medal made this game very frustrating to play. To get a gold medal, you have to make no mistakes at all for the whole day. Remembering that I said this game has a "relatively" low down time compared to its first installment? Getting all gold medal for every stage greatly amplifies those down time, because for the 6 and a half minutes of gameplay, only around 2 minutes during the rush hours are remotely challenging, and failing just one single dish means you had just essentially wasted a couple minutes of your life accomplishing nothing other than staring at the empty screen waiting for customers to arrive and rush hours to end. I hate how every single subtle failure becomes a reminder of my time wasted on a level.

I can't express how much I despise this game for its various problems but still want to finish it, and this mindset made me hate this game even more. I wish I had never bought it in the first place.

Not nearly as much fun as the first game. The addition of some new foods and the ability to work in other restaurants to gain experience is appreciated, but it has some serious bugs. For one, the video options simply DON'T WORK. Also, sometimes when you prepare a food for the keep warm counter, it IMMEDIATELY goes bad and earns you a negative rating which you can't do anything about.

It's also frustrating that you HAVE to turn the menu over to access the second or third page of toppings, even when you know the key to press. You can't just press K for ketchup, you HAVE to flip the page, and only then will the button actually do anything. Why?

Stick with the original. It's cheaper and better.

This is one of those games that while it looks odd, it's a lot of fun. It's really charming and genuinely fun! I prefer THIS game to both 1 and 3. 

In general, this is a management game.

Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! is almost a typing game in that you need precise, quick key presses in order to do well in the serving of different dishes. You read what the customer wants (if applicable) and execute the dish correctly. It's fast-paced, and in the upper levels, can be difficult. The charm of the emails and item descriptions give the "story" fun tidbits as you go through different levels and challenges. 

You can play on your own restaurant, where you purchase dishes you want to put on the menu to execute and earn money from others, or you can be a hired chef at other restaurants. Personally, I find this second section really fun. The gameplay shines here! I enjoy the challenge of earning gold medals (all perfect orders and no missed chores), especially in some of the restaurants where each dish is highly customizable. Once you learn some of the patterns, it gets easier. It's not unfair, just really specific. You kinda get to pick your difficulty, which I think is cool.

Overall, this is a fun, personal-challenge type management game. Worth the chance if you're not sure about it! It's weird - in a good way. One of my favorites.

If you've ever wondered what it's like to run a high-pressure kitchen while an avalanche of orders rains down on you, Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! delivers the experience with all the intensity of a service rush at a five-star restaurant—and none of the clean-up.

A sequel to the indie darling Cook, Serve, Delicious!, this entry dramatically expands the menu, adds new restaurant settings, and introduces cooperative gameplay. It's bigger, harder, and—when everything's clicking—more satisfying than ever.

What’s Cooking:
-Addictive Gameplay Loop: Every level throws dozens of food orders at you, and your job is to prep, cook, and serve them under strict time constraints. It’s part memory game, part reflex test, and part chaos management. When you're in the zone, it's pure adrenaline.
-Massive Content: With over 400 food items and dozens of restaurants to work in (each with their own themes and challenges), the variety is staggering. From burgers and sushi to more complex dishes like empanadas and gumbo, there's always something new to learn.
-Local Co-Op Mode: Working together in the kitchen is either a great bonding experience or the fastest path to yelling “YOU FORGOT THE TOFU!” at your best friend. Either way, it’s hilarious and genuinely fun.
-Customization Galore: You can design your own restaurant’s look, pick your own menus, and replay levels to earn medals. It adds a nice personal touch to the chaos.

What’s Undercooked:
-Steep Difficulty Curve: The game doesn’t hold back. If you’re not quick on the keys (or controller), it can quickly become overwhelming. While there is a Chill Mode, casual players may still feel the pressure.
-Repetition: Though the food variety is massive, the core gameplay doesn’t evolve much across levels. After a while, it can feel like you're grinding the same motions, albeit with different dishes.
-UI Learning Curve: The menu navigation and dish selection interface can be a little clunky, especially when starting out or playing with a controller.

Cook, Serve, Delicious! 2!! is a stress simulator disguised as a cooking game—and that’s exactly what makes it great. For players who love multitasking under pressure, chasing high scores, and fine-tuning their muscle memory, this is a five-star dish. It’s not for the faint of heart, but for those who thrive on organized chaos, it’s a feast.

A spicy, fast-paced sequel that serves up intensity with every order. Best enjoyed hot—and with a good timer.

Rating: 8/10

An amazing improvement over Cook, Serve, Delicious!.

Most significant is the introduction of holding stations, where you can prepare dishes and side dishes. Not all dishes can be prepared like that though. Side dishes increase customer patience, so you often have to choose what to do with the limited amounts of holding stations.
The maximum amount of "prep stations" (the orders coming in from the left) has been increased to 14, which is very daunting.. You'll be using -=[] to access those, and I think that's mostly why CSD2 is much harder than CSD1.

The writing has become even better. I laughed a lot at the dish descriptions and the restaurant About me's. They have this very absurd humor. reminds me a bit of Hitchhiker's guide to the galaxy.
The intro "song" is even better than CSD1's. funniest part is always when the girl says Dulleeeeeshus with that voice. like.. why does she say it like that?!..
The soundtrack has expanded a bit from CSD1. It's a nice and happy soundtrack that fits the game, and I'll be nicely and happily buying it in the next sale.

Some critique:
- as others have said, there's no way to redo an order after making a mistake. but what's even worse and more often the case, you don't even know that you did something wrong until you send the order and the customer is not very happy. The game should provide better feedback imo. Instead I use Radeon Relive to clip the last 30 seconds and rewatch what I did exactly to figure out I missed a key or confused some ingredients.
- there's no way to .. move the window ?.. The game is stuck centered in the middle without the typical white bar on top that allows you to move the game window. a very strange oversight. On the plus side, the game is now 1080p instead of CSD1's 720p.

minor issues:
- hard to find a dish because there's so many, and there's only pictures, no search function or any text. I think I needed 10 minutes to gather 6 dishes that were required for the achievement. It was also not clear at first that I had to buy dish recipes, because some dishes are automatically unlocked as you level up (without having to buy its recipe).
- the achievements are a little inconsistent. There's achievements for some restaurants, not for others. It's also weird how they only pop after closing the game.

oh well. time for CSD3 let's go!

This game is a great balance between challenging and comfort. You assemble dishes, drinks, and perform other tasks in a kitchen where each ingredient or individual action is bound to a specific key on the keyboard. After playing on and off for years now, I think I have a section of my brain and muscle memory dedicated solely to assembling certain dishes from this game. The food artwork and decorations are lovely, though the space you get to decorate is rather constricted. There's a good variety of different foods and restaurants. If you like cooking sims or are looking for a game to help with typing speed and finger muscle memory, I would highly recommend the CSD series.
